tldr: High-accuracy Hamilton-Jacobi reachability analysis, long considered strictly an offline computation due to heavy workloads, can now run at up to over one hundred Hz through GPU-tailored algorithmic optimizations, bringing certified safety guarantees directly into a robot's real-time control loop.
hero_caption: A closed-loop simulation of six quadcopters tackling a 20 km × 20 km wildfire under spatiotemporally varying wind fields. Reachable areas (Voronoi partitions) from each drone's current position are recomputed in real time via a single HJ solve at each control cycle (10 Hz) to make optimal dispatch decisions.
overview:
Recent autonomy stacks—including ADAS/AV, humanoid robotics, and vision-language-action (VLA) models—increasingly rely on large learned policies for decision-making. However, these models are inherently probabilistic black boxes that cannot formally certify worst-case safety. A reliable tool to address this is Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis, which computes backward reachable tubes (BRTs) that mathematically guarantee safe state sets even under worst-case disturbances.

Yet, level-set methods for computing BRTs suffer from exponential scaling with state dimension. Historically, the only practical option was to compute them offline for hours and look up fixed value tables during execution. In real-world environments, road friction, wind gusts, obstacles, and dynamics change continuously. A static BRT quickly becomes obsolete when conditions shift.

This paper overturns that assumption. Building on the canonical high-order scheme (WENO5 + TVD-RK3 + Lax-Friedrichs), the authors developed a CUDA solver thoroughly tuned for modern GPU cache hierarchies via full kernel fusion, algebraic division reduction, and static CFL stepping. In single precision (FP32) on a workstation GPU (NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada), it solves the 3D Air3D problem at 112 Hz and a 4D pursuit-evasion problem at 61 Hz—fast enough for inner-loop control. Furthermore, on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, it operates at tens of Hz within an approximate 31 W power budget.

This opens the door to a new paradigm of robotic safety layers: recomputing fresh, certified safety sets on the fly at every single control tick as the environment and robot state evolve.
contributions: Implemented an online CUDA solver for the canonical high-order level-set HJ scheme (WENO5 + TVD-RK3), solving 3D problems at 112 Hz and 4D problems at 61 Hz directly inside a robot control loop.

Achieved massive speedups—several-fold to over an order of magnitude faster than standard libraries like JAX/hj_reachability and torch.compile—by exploiting L2 cache direct fetches, eliminating WENO5 divisions, and fusing RK3 stages.
Demonstrated real-time onboard capability on a low-power embedded platform (NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor) running Air3D at 66 Hz under roughly 31 W of power consumption.

Proposed an in-kernel label-propagation technique that recovers multi-agent time-to-reach Voronoi tessellations from a single HJ solve in time independent of fleet size, verifying it in a closed-loop wildfire-response simulation with six quadcopters under time-varying winds.

sections.heading: Giving black-box AI a real-time mathematical safety shield
sections.summary: Autonomous robots powered by VLAs and deep models require a deterministic layer to guarantee worst-case safety. This section highlights why breaking the offline speed barrier of HJ reachability matters and how recomputing safety every cycle changes the game.
sections.details:
Modern autonomous systems—such as ADAS/AV stacks, humanoid robots, and vision-language-action (VLA) models—are increasingly driven by deep neural network policies. However, these policies are inherently probabilistic, meaning worst-case catastrophic failures cannot be ruled out beforehand. This creates an urgent need for a model-based, deterministic safety layer capable of mathematically guaranteeing worst-case safety.

The gold standard theoretical tool for this is Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis. It yields a Backward Reachable Tube (BRT), which characterizes the exact set of initial states that will inevitably enter a hazard set under worst-case disturbances. Intervening with a safe control action the instant the system touches this boundary prevents catastrophic failures.

However, level-set solvers for BRTs battle the curse of dimensionality and carry high computational burdens. Historically, computing BRTs was restricted to offline runs, after which the robot queried static look-up tables. Yet real-world conditions like wind gusts, shifting obstacles, and changing robot dynamics rapidly invalidate static BRTs.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed a CUDA solver that brings reachability computation online. Using single-precision floating point (FP32) on an RTX 4000 Ada, it solves the 3D Air3D pursuit problem at 112 Hz and a 4D pursuit-evasion problem at 61 Hz. This enables an entirely new design pattern: recomputing safety boundaries from scratch at every control step rather than once per mission.

sections.heading: The foundations of Hamilton-Jacobi equations and level-set methods
sections.summary: This section outlines the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) PDE formulation modeling minimax games between control inputs and worst-case disturbances, using standard 5th-order spatial and 3rd-order temporal numerical schemes.
sections.details:
Consider a nonlinear dynamical system $\dot{x} = f(x,u,d)$ with state $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, control input $u \in \mathcal{U}$, and disturbance $d \in \mathcal{D}$. Defining an obstacle or target set as the zero sublevel set of a signed distance function $\ell(x)$, the Backward Reachable Tube (BRT) is the set of all states from which the system can be driven into the hazard within time horizon $T$ under worst-case disturbances.

Foundational work by Mitchell et al. shows that this BRT can be represented as the zero sublevel set of a value function $V(t,x)$. This function satisfies a Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) partial differential equation integrated backward in time from the terminal condition $V(0,x) = \ell(x)$.

The Hamiltonian $H(x,p)$ captures a worst-case differential game where control acts to maximize safety while disturbances act maliciously. To solve this PDE on a uniform Cartesian grid, the authors employ the canonical numerical recipe: 5th-order weighted essentially non-oscillatory reconstruction (WENO5) for spatial derivatives, a 3rd-order total variation diminishing Runge-Kutta scheme (TVD-RK3) for time marching, and Lax-Friedrichs numerical flux dissipation with a CFL condition controlling the time step. To ensure the value function is monotonically non-increasing over backward time, Mitchell's BRT clamp, $V \leftarrow \min(V_{\text{new}}, V_{\text{old}})$, is applied at each step.

sections.heading: Finding the sweet spot between exact classical solvers and neural approximations
sections.summary: Prior work split into accurate but strictly offline classical tools versus fast but unverified neural approximations. This research fills the missing gap by delivering classical accuracy at robot control rates.
sections.details:
The lineage of classical HJ reachability tools stems from Mitchell's ToolboxLS in MATLAB and its C++/CUDA port, BEACLS. Stanford ASL's modern JAX/XLA rewrite, hj_reachability, has since become the standard benchmark. While these tools offer provable mathematical convergence, runtimes range from seconds to minutes or even hours, precluding online execution in control loops.

To circumvent this bottleneck, recent work has explored neural network approximations of value functions (such as DeepReach), grid-free Hopf formula evaluations for pointwise solutions, and MPC-based predictive safety filters. However, while neural networks offer fast inference, they struggle to provide rigorous worst-case guarantees. Pointwise methods, on the other hand, cannot reconstruct the full spatial boundary at once.

This paper targets the intersection of both paradigms: retaining the mathematical convergence guarantees of high-order classical grid solvers while unleashing modern GPU architectures to finish the solve within onboard robot control periods (tens of Hz).

sections.heading: Kernel-level secrets that squeeze maximum performance out of GPUs
sections.summary: The solver achieves extreme speed not through algorithmic shortcuts, but through rigorous hardware-aligned optimizations: kernel fusion, WENO5 division elimination, and relying on the L2 cache for direct fetches.
sections.details:
The solver supports 2D, 3D, and 4D dynamics, written in templated CUDA code for both single (float) and double precision (double). The core engineering decisions driving its performance include:

### IV-A Discretization Scheme
Spatial derivatives use Jiang and Peng's WENO5 scheme, accessing a 6-cell stencil per axis. Time marching uses Shu and Osher's TVD-RK3, strictly bounded by the CFL condition ($\Delta t \cdot \alpha_{\max} / \Delta x \le 0.75$).

### IV-B GPU Kernel Structure and Optimization Techniques
- **Full Kernel Fusion Per RK3 Stage**: In each Runge-Kutta stage, WENO5 reconstruction along all axes, Lax-Friedrichs Hamiltonian evaluation, stage combination, and final BRT clamping are fused into a single kernel operating entirely in registers. This eliminates intermediate global memory round-trips.
- **In-Place Updates to Avoid Buffer Copies**: In RK3 stage 3, stencils are read from the stage 2 buffer, and output values overwrite the base array in-place, eliminating memory copies between time steps.
- **Bypassing Shared Memory for Direct L2 Cache Fetches**: Standard stencil codes usually load tiles into Shared Memory. Here, the solver uses direct global memory fetches. Grid sizes fitting within robot control constraints (e.g., $101^3$ in FP32 is ~4 MB) fit entirely inside modern GPU L2 caches (40 MB on the RTX 4000 Ada). Shared memory introduced halo-loading and thread-sync overhead, running roughly $3\times$ slower.
- **Algebraic Elimination of WENO5 Divisions**: Textbook WENO5 requires 13 floating-point divisions per cell. By cross-multiplying common denominators across weight normalization steps, divisions are reduced to exactly one per axis. Because consumer GPUs have limited double-precision division units, this yields dramatic speedups.
- **Host-Determined CFL Stepping**: Since the maximum wave speed $\alpha_{\max}$ is time-invariant or separable across coordinates in target Hamiltonians, whole-grid GPU reductions are eliminated. In the 3D solver, all three RK kernels and time stepping are captured as a CUDA Graph, reducing host launch latency to zero.

### IV-C Boundary Conditions and Constraints
Neumann and periodic boundary conditions are evaluated inline during memory access. In addition, obstacle masking and reach-while-avoid post-processing clamps are supported directly inside the fused kernels.

sections.heading: Cross-verification protocol against the gold standard: hj_reachability
sections.summary: To confirm that the accelerated solver produces mathematically sound results, the authors executed cross-library verifications against Stanford ASL's JAX reference hj_reachability across eight benchmark cases.
sections.details:
To prove the solver does not compromise accuracy for speed, direct comparisons were run against Stanford ASL's open-source JAX reference (hj_reachability). Eight benchmark problems spanning 2D, 3D, and 4D dynamics were codified in identical JSON problem definitions on identical grids.

Verification was performed in FP64 (double precision), setting `jax_enable_x64=True` in JAX, using matching WENO5, TVD-RK3, global Lax-Friedrichs dissipation, and a CFL factor of 0.75.

Minor implementation differences were accounted for. For instance, this solver applies BRT clamping after all three RK3 stages complete ($V^{n+1} \leftarrow \min(V^{n+1}, V^n)$), whereas hj_reachability clamps intermediate Hamiltonian updates during each Euler sub-stage. In the 4D pursuit-evasion problem, this solver uses gradient-local dissipation and linear boundary extrapolation, whereas JAX uses global coefficients and zero-Neumann boundaries. Once aligned, cell-count agreement between the two libraries reached within 0.3% to 0.6%, validating the verification protocol.

sections.heading: Benchmark results: Crushing existing tools with millisecond-scale reachability
sections.summary: After verifying FP64 precision, performance was evaluated in FP32. On a workstation GPU, the solver solved 3D Air3D at 112 Hz and 4D pursuit-evasion at 61 Hz, outperforming JAX by up to 17.5x and torch.compile by up to 16x.
sections.details:
### VI-A Cross-Library Precision and FP64 Performance
In FP64, the solver was benchmarked against hj_reachability and an optimized `torch.compile` implementation of the same scheme. Across all benchmarks, point-wise maximum errors ($L_\infty$) were negligible, verifying exact mathematical agreement. In terms of runtime, the handwritten CUDA kernels were 2.0–4.6× faster than JAX and 1.3–1.4× faster than `torch.compile`.

### VI-B Reproducing Mitchell's Air3D Benchmark
In Mitchell's canonical 3D Air3D pursuit-evasion problem with a 5 m collision radius, the computed BRT cell count on an $N=51$ grid (~11,200 cells) differed from JAX by only 4 cells (0.04%), showing near-perfect agreement.

### VI-C Equi-Accuracy Speedup
Measuring the computational time required to hit a target $L_\infty$ error across varying grid resolutions, the proposed solver achieved target accuracy 3.1–4.9× faster than JAX in every tested configuration.

### VI-D Real-Time FP32 Performance
In FP32 mode—the target for onboard robot control—division reduction and cache residency delivered 21–33× speedups over FP64. Compared to JAX in FP32, it was 5.9–17.5× faster, and 1.7–16× faster than `torch.compile`.
- **3D Air3D**: $N=51$ completed in 8.9 ms (112 Hz).
- **4D Pursuit-Evasion**: Over 1 million cells ($31^4$) solved in 16 ms (61 Hz).
- **2D Drifter**: $N=200$ ran at 74–147 Hz.

This proves that BRTs no longer need static offline lookup tables; they can be recomputed from scratch inside 10–100 Hz inner control loops.

sections.heading: Multi-agent fleet dispatch: Fighting wildfires under turbulent winds
sections.summary: As a real-world multi-agent test, the solver managed drone fleet dispatches under non-uniform, shifting wind gusts. By embedding label propagation inside a single HJ solve, fleet reachability was resolved in a constant 4 ms regardless of drone count.
sections.details:
### VII-A & VII-B Problem Setup and the Need for Level-Set Reachability
A fleet of six quadcopters (cruising speed 20 m/s) was simulated over a 20 km × 20 km area with moving, rotational wind gusts reaching up to 30 m/s. Under non-uniform, time-varying wind, standard Euclidean Voronoi partitioning fails completely. Solving level-set reachability governed by the drift PDE is necessary to capture accurate arrival times.

### VII-C In-Kernel Label Propagation: $K$ Agents at the Cost of One
Normally, computing reachable basins for $K$ drones requires $K$ independent HJ solves, scaling linearly with fleet size. However, when agents share identical dynamics, the minimum value function $\min_i V_i(t,x)$ satisfies the exact same PDE.

The authors implemented "in-kernel label propagation": when the earliest arriving wavefront hits a cell, an integer label denoting the owner drone is propagated from neighbor cells during the update. This recovers the multi-agent Voronoi partition in a single combined pass at only ~1.3× the computational cost of one drone, independent of fleet size $K$. Compared to running six separate solves (69–77 ms), the unified pass took 15–17 ms (a 4.6× speedup) and achieved 99.5% label agreement with individual argmin evaluations.

### VII-D & VII-E Closed-Loop Simulation Results
A 10-minute reachable horizon Voronoi partition was recomputed every tick in a 10 Hz outer control loop, taking just 4.0 ms per solve (~250 Hz throughput). As drones dispatched and moved, their Voronoi territories dynamically stretched and adapted to wind patterns, successfully dispatching optimal quadcopters to all three wildfire outbreaks without delay.

captions.F4: Closed-loop wildfire response simulation with six quadcopters in strong wind fields. Each drone's real-time capture basin (color-coded Voronoi cells) and unreachable areas within the horizon (red hatching) adapt continuously to shifting winds and drone motion.

sections.heading: Limitations, embedded Jetson benchmarks, and next steps
sections.summary: This section examines the 4D curse-of-dimensionality boundary, evaluates performance on an embedded Jetson AGX Thor at 31 W, and discusses future applications in VLAs and autonomous driving.
sections.details:
### VIII-A The 4D Dimensionality Wall
While this work dramatically lowers the constant-factor compute costs, it does not erase the curse of dimensionality inherent in grid-based level-set schemes. Even in FP32, a 4D grid ($51^4 \approx 6.8 \times 10^6$ cells) takes 0.22 s, which falls outside a 30 Hz control cycle. Going beyond 4D still requires subspace decomposition or hybrid neural methods.

### VIII-B Precision in Single Precision (FP32)
In 2D and 3D, FP32 BRT classifications matched FP64 ground truth perfectly. In 4D, disagreement was under 0.1%. Because boundary cells can fluctuate slightly due to floating-point precision, incorporating a one-cell boundary uncertainty buffer is recommended in practice.

### VIII-C Performance on Embedded Jetson AGX Thor
To evaluate onboard robotic suitability, tests were conducted on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor SoC (Blackwell architecture) using the exact same codebase. Under a roughly 31 W power envelope, 3D Air3D ($N=41$) ran at 66 Hz, 2D drifter at 54 Hz, and 4D pursuit-evasion ($N=31$) at 19 Hz. The wildfire Voronoi solve completed in ~10 ms (~100 Hz), proving that real-time execution on embedded robotics hardware is entirely viable.

### VIII-D Why Handwritten CUDA Beats General Compilers (torch.compile)
General-purpose tensor compilers break array operations into smaller elementwise kernels. They cannot infer scheme-specific mathematical transformations like eliminating WENO5 divisions, eliminating CFL reductions via time-invariance, or leveraging L2 cache residency over shared memory. These domain-specific insights give handwritten CUDA a strong edge.

### VIII-E Future Applications
This breakthrough paves the way for real-time safety filters monitoring VLA model commands, online collision avoidance adapting to changing road friction in autonomous driving, and balance recovery for humanoids walking over rough, dynamic terrain.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Turning safety guarantees from offline artifacts into real-time shields
sections.summary: By engineering a GPU-tailored solver for canonical high-order level-set HJI equations, BRT computations can now run directly inside robot control loops, providing an adaptive deterministic safety layer for learning-based autonomous systems.
sections.details:
This work introduced an online CUDA implementation of the canonical WENO5 + TVD-RK3 + Lax-Friedrichs level-set Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs solver, running fast enough on both workstation GPUs and embedded SoCs (Jetson AGX Thor) to sit directly within robot control loops.

After demonstrating strict numerical agreement with hj_reachability in FP64, the FP32 solver achieved refresh rates ranging from tens to over one hundred Hz. Moreover, in-kernel label propagation enabled multi-agent Voronoi partitioning at speeds independent of fleet size.

This marks a transition for formal safety guarantees in ADAS, humanoid robotics, and VLA policies—transforming Hamilton-Jacobi reachability from a static offline computation into a dynamic, real-time safety layer that continuously adapts to changing real-world conditions.

takeaways: High-accuracy Hamilton-Jacobi reachability analysis, historically limited to offline tools, can now run inside 10–100 Hz robot control loops using optimized GPU kernels.
For grid sizes constrained by real-time control deadlines, bypassing Shared Memory in favor of direct L2 cache fetches can yield significantly higher performance on modern GPUs.

Exploiting the mathematical structure of the PDE—such as eliminating WENO5 divisions and using static CFL bounds—provides performance advantages that general tensor compilers like torch.compile cannot match.
Multi-agent reachability for identical dynamics can be mapped into a single wavefront pass with in-kernel label propagation, recovering Voronoi partitions in $O(1)$ time relative to fleet size.
limitations: The solver does not eliminate the exponential curse of dimensionality; standalone real-time solves remain bounded at around 4D state spaces.
Single-precision (FP32) evaluations exhibit minor classification fluctuations (<0.1%) right at the tube boundary compared to FP64, requiring small safety margins in practice.
Current pipelines retain minor CPU-to-GPU transfer overheads when updating time-varying dynamics and environmental parameters at each step.
